Concurrency: go, Channels, and Shared State

SLA's concurrency rule is structural: borrows never cross a task boundary (the checker rejects both the go form and the thread::spawn closure form — see the &mut comparison page). What crosses is an owned value: a channel end, or an Arc clone. The four programs on this page are the verified shapes.

go and a Channel Round-Trip

Chan::new(0) creates a rendezvous channel; recv() returns a (value, closed) pair; go starts a task and sa_task_join(h) collects its status:

@import "sa_std/task.sai"
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn double_worker(ch: Chan<u64>) {
    let (v, closed) = ch.recv();
    if closed { panic(9701); };
    ch.send(v * 2);
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let ch: Chan<u64> = Chan::new(0);
    let h = go double_worker(ch);
    ch.send(21);
    let (r, closed) = ch.recv();
    if closed { return 1; };
    let st = sa_task_join(h);
    if st != 0 { return 2; };
    println("{}", r);
    ch.destroy();
    if r != 42 { return 3; };
    return 0;
}

Verified output: 42, exit code 0 — the worker doubled the 21 it received and sent it back over the same channel.

thread::spawn and a Two-Channel Ping-Pong

With thread::spawn, the spawned closure takes ownership of what it captures. Here the worker owns both channel ends and answers 50 requests:

@import "sa_std/task.sai"
@import "sa_std/thread.sa"
@import "sa_std/core/result.sa"
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn pp_worker(req: Chan<u64>, resp: Chan<u64>) {
    let i = 0;
    while i < 50 {
        let (v, closed) = req.recv();
        if closed { panic(9601); };
        resp.send(v + 1);
        i = i + 1;
    }
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let req: Chan<u64> = Chan::new(0);
    let resp: Chan<u64> = Chan::new(0);
    let h = thread::spawn(^|| pp_worker(req, resp));
    let i = 0;
    let last: u64 = 0;
    while i < 50 {
        req.send(i as u64);
        let (r, closed) = resp.recv();
        if closed { panic(9602); };
        last = r;
        i = i + 1;
    }
    let jr = h.join();
    println("{}", last);
    req.destroy();
    resp.destroy();
    if last != 50 { return 1; };
    return 0;
}

Verified output: 50, exit code 0 — the last reply of 50 request/response rounds, each side checking the closed flag on every receive.

Shared State: Arc<Mutex<i32>>

Four workers, 250 increments each, one shared counter:

@import "sa_std/core/arc.sa"
@import "sa_std/sync/mutex.sa"
@import "sa_std/thread.sa"
@import "sa_std/core/result.sa"
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn worker(counter: Arc<Mutex<i32>>) -> i32 {
    let i = 0;
    while i < 250 {
        let guard = (*counter).lock().unwrap();
        let cur = *guard;
        *guard = cur + 1;
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return 1;
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));
    let c1 = counter.clone();
    let c2 = counter.clone();
    let c3 = counter.clone();
    let c4 = counter.clone();
    let a = thread::spawn(^|| worker(c1));
    let b = thread::spawn(^|| worker(c2));
    let c = thread::spawn(^|| worker(c3));
    let d = thread::spawn(^|| worker(c4));
    let s = a.join().unwrap() + b.join().unwrap() + c.join().unwrap() + d.join().unwrap();
    let guard = (*counter).lock().unwrap();
    let final = *guard;
    println("{}", final);
    if s != 4 { return 2; };
    if final != 1000 { return 1; };
    return 0;
}

Verified output: exactly 1000, exit code 0. The clones are made explicitly (counter.clone()) and moved into the spawned closures; the guard pattern — lock().unwrap(), read, write, drop — mirrors Rust.

Shared State: Arc<RwLock<i32>>

One writer adding 2 a hundred times, two readers asserting every value they observe is even:

@import "sa_std/core/arc.sa"
@import "sa_std/sync/rwlock.sa"
@import "sa_std/thread.sa"
@import "sa_std/core/result.sa"
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn writer(lock: Arc<RwLock<i32>>) -> i32 {
    let i = 0;
    while i < 100 {
        let g = (*lock).write().unwrap();
        let cur = *g;
        *g = cur + 2;
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return 1;
}

fn reader(lock: Arc<RwLock<i32>>) -> i32 {
    let seen = 0;
    let done = 0;
    while done == 0 {
        let g = (*lock).read().unwrap();
        let v = *g;
        if v % 2 != 0 { panic(4101); };
        if v > seen { seen = v; };
        if v >= 200 { done = 1; };
    }
    return seen;
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let lock = Arc::new(RwLock::new(0));
    let w = lock.clone();
    let r1 = lock.clone();
    let r2 = lock.clone();
    let hw = thread::spawn(^|| writer(w));
    let h1 = thread::spawn(^|| reader(r1));
    let h2 = thread::spawn(^|| reader(r2));
    let sw = hw.join().unwrap();
    let s1 = h1.join().unwrap();
    let s2 = h2.join().unwrap();
    let g = (*lock).read().unwrap();
    let final = *g;
    println("{}", final);
    if sw != 1 { return 2; };
    if s1 != 200 { return 3; };
    if s2 != 200 { return 4; };
    if final != 200 { return 1; };
    return 0;
}

This program passed verification, printing 200 with exit code 0. Report it honestly, though: in the longer measurement series on the comparison page, the same writer/reader shape printed 200 in 22 of 28 runs and ended in a runtime panic (code 17) in the other 6 — the RwLock mix is timing-sensitive today, while the channel handoff and the Mutex counter above were exact in every run. Prefer channels and Mutex for new code until that changes.

Key Points of This Page

  • Borrows do not cross task boundaries; owned values do — channel ends and Arc clones.
  • go + Chan::new(0) + sa_task_join is the lightest task shape; recv() yields (value, closed).
  • Arc<Mutex<i32>> with four workers produced exactly 1000.
  • The RwLock reader/writer mix reaches 200 but is timing-sensitive in longer runs (22 of 28 clean); channels and Mutex were exact in every run.
